nameStory: Eelgrass gets its name from its long, ribbon-like leaves that sway gracefully underwater like swimming eels. When storms tear the grass loose from the seafloor, it washes ashore as "seawrack" - a much less poetic name for this underwater meadow plant that has fed coastal communities for centuries.
description: Eelgrass is a true flowering plant that lives completely underwater in shallow coastal areas, forming vast underwater meadows in bays and estuaries. Its long, flat, ribbon-like leaves grow in clusters from creeping underground stems called rhizomes, creating dense green carpets on sandy or muddy sea bottoms. Individual leaves can stretch several feet long and about half an inch wide, swaying gently with the tides and currents.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, flat, ribbon-like leaves that feel smooth and slightly rubbery, bright to dark green underwater, growing in clusters from the base

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense underwater meadows connected by creeping rhizomes (underground stems) that anchor the plants in soft sediment

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous flowers hidden within protective leaf sheaths - you'll rarely notice them without close inspection

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, oval seeds that float and can wash up on beaches, often found mixed in with seaweed wrack

habitat: Shallow saltwater areas along New England's coast, including protected bays, estuaries, salt ponds, and tidal flats. Eelgrass thrives in sandy or muddy bottoms in water depths from just below low tide to about 20 feet deep, where sunlight can still reach the seafloor. You'll find the densest beds in areas protected from heavy wave action.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as water temperatures warm, with fresh green shoots appearing from overwintered rhizomes. This is when underwater meadows begin to thicken and expand.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush, dense underwater meadows at their fullest. Tiny flowers bloom underwater during warmer months, though they're easily missed.
seasonality.fall: Older leaves begin to break free and wash ashore as seawrack - those tangles of ribbon-like seaweed you see on beaches. Seeds mature and disperse with currents.
seasonality.winter: Many leaves die back, but the underground rhizomes survive under the sediment, ready to sprout new growth when spring returns.

funFact: Eelgrass meadows are one of the most productive ecosystems on Earth, producing more oxygen per square foot than tropical rainforests, and a single acre can support over 40,000 fish and countless shellfish, crabs, and other marine life.
confusionNotes: When washed ashore as seawrack, eelgrass is often mistaken for seaweed, but unlike true seaweeds (which are algae), eelgrass has distinct parallel veins running lengthwise through its leaves and was once rooted in sediment rather than attached to rocks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "grass," eelgrass isn't related to lawn grass at all - it's actually more closely related to pond weeds and wild celery. Many coastal New Englanders historically used dried eelgrass for insulation, mattress stuffing, and even thatching roofs.
compareHints: Eelgrass is the only common seagrass species in New England waters. Other marine plants you might encounter include various brown, red, and green seaweeds (which are algae, not flowering plants), but these typically attach to rocks rather than growing rooted in sediment, and lack the distinct parallel leaf veins of eelgrass.
